label: Itchy eczematous dermatitis
lead: Eczema is a reaction pattern, not a diagnosis. The pattern is set by the cause, and the cause is usually written in the distribution. Read the map before you read the morphology: where it is tells you more than what it looks like.

stop.l: Erythroderma — confluent erythema over more than 90% of the surface
stop.a: Admit. Fluid, protein and thermoregulatory losses, and secondary sepsis, are the risks. Establish the underlying cause.

stop.l: Monomorphic punched-out erosions on eczematous skin, with fever
stop.a: Eczema herpeticum. Systemic acyclovir now. Regularly misread as bacterial superinfection and treated with antibiotics alone while it disseminates.

stop.l: Sudden severe dermatitis with weight loss or lymphadenopathy in an older adult
stop.a: Consider cutaneous T cell lymphoma or an internal malignancy. Biopsy, and examine the nodes.

stop.l: Widespread crusting, honey-colored exudate, and fever
stop.a: Bacterial superinfection or streptococcal cellulitis on a barrier-defective skin. Swab and treat systemically.

stop.l: Dermatitis with burrows in a resident of an institution or a household outbreak
stop.a: Scabies, possibly crusted scabies if immunosuppressed. Treat the patient and all contacts simultaneously, and consider public health implications.

stop.l: Periorificial and acral erosive dermatitis with diarrhea, alopecia and irritability in an infant
stop.a: Zinc deficiency. Send serum zinc but start elemental zinc replacement immediately - diarrhea and mood improve within 24 hours and the skin within 1 to 2 weeks. Untreated acrodermatitis enteropathica is fatal, and the same picture in an adult means malabsorption, alcohol dependence or unsupplemented parenteral nutrition.

dx.look: Dry, cracked skin with a red, fissured crazy-paving (crazed-porcelain) pattern, typically on the shins of older adults in winter or low-humidity settings; it is intensely itchy and prone to secondary eczematization.
fr: Crazy-paving or dried-riverbed pattern of fine red fissures
Shins of older adults, worse in winter or dry heat
Marked xerosis of the surrounding skin
Rapid improvement with emollients
Overwashing or diuretic use in the history
ag: Sharply marginated silvery plaques
Central clearing with an advancing edge
Vesicles on the palms and soles
dx.cf: A clinical diagnosis - the crazy-paving pattern on xerotic shins is characteristic; consider hypothyroidism, zinc deficiency or a lymphoma-associated cause if severe and refractory.
dx.hp: Mild spongiotic dermatitis with compact hyperkeratosis and a poorly hydrated stratum corneum; biopsy is rarely needed.
dx.assoc: Precipitated by low humidity, overwashing, diuretics and aging skin; severe or refractory disease should prompt thought about hypothyroidism, zinc deficiency or an underlying lymphoma.
dx.mgmt: Liberal emollients and reduced washing are the cornerstone, with a short course of a mid-potency topical corticosteroid ointment for the inflammation; humidify the environment.

dx.look: A symmetric, itchy, papulovesicular eczematous eruption at sites distant from a primary focus of inflammation or infection - classically vesicles on the sides of the fingers in response to tinea pedis, or a flare around a stasis dermatitis or infected wound.
fr: Symmetric distant eruption following a primary dermatitis or infection
Vesicles on the sides of the fingers or palms with active tinea pedis
Onset after a flare or superinfection of the primary site
Clears when the primary focus is treated
Intense itch
ag: A single localized plaque
A positive KOH at the eruption itself
No identifiable primary focus
dx.cf: Identify and treat the primary focus (tinea, stasis dermatitis, infected wound) and the id reaction resolves; KOH of the distant lesions is negative.
dx.hp: Spongiotic dermatitis without an organism at the site - a reactive eczema; the pathology is at the primary focus, not the id lesions.
dx.assoc: A reactive hypersensitivity to a distant focus - most often tinea pedis, but also stasis dermatitis, infected wounds or a retained suture; treating the focus resolves the eruption.
dx.mgmt: Treat the primary trigger (antifungal for tinea, antibiotics for infection), with topical corticosteroids and emollients for the id eruption itself.

dx.look: Chronic relapsing pruritic dermatitis with age-defined distribution: cheeks and extensors in infancy, flexural antecubital and popliteal in childhood and adulthood, with lichenification, xerosis and Dennie-Morgan folds. Personal or family history of asthma, hay fever or food allergy.
fr: Flexural distribution in a child or adult, facial and extensor in an infant
Personal or family history of atopy
Chronic and relapsing since childhood
Xerosis with lichenification
Itch precedes the rash — the itch that rashes
ag: Sharply marginated to an area of contact
Adult onset with no atopic history
Burrows in finger webs
dx.cf: Clinical, on the pattern and history. Patch testing when an adult atopic patient deteriorates or the distribution changes — superimposed allergic contact dermatitis to topical treatments is common and easily missed.
dx.hp: Spongiotic dermatitis with acanthosis and a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate; chronic lesions show lichenification.
dx.assoc: Part of the atopic triad (asthma, allergic rhinitis), with filaggrin loss-of-function and barrier dysfunction. Staphylococcus aureus superinfection and eczema herpeticum drive flares.
dx.mgmt: Emollients with topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors and trigger avoidance; step up to phototherapy, dupilumab or a JAK inhibitor for moderate-to-severe disease.

dx.look: Erythema, papules then vesicles, appearing 12–72 hours after re-exposure. Initially sharply confined to the site of contact with the allergen, then spreading into the surrounding skin and sometimes generalizing. Itch dominates, later pain. Often linear or geometric — an outside job.
fr: Delayed onset, 12–72 hours after exposure
Begins sharply marginated at the contact site, then spreads beyond
Geometric, linear or artificial outlines
Papules present in the acute phase
Occurs only in sensitized individuals, at very low doses
ag: Immediate stinging within minutes of contact
Strictly confined to contact site with no spreading
Symmetric flexural pattern from childhood
dx.cf: Patch testing is the definitive test, applied for 48 hours with reads at 48 and 96 hours. Delay until the dermatitis has been quiet for at least 2 weeks and apply to previously uninvolved skin.
dx.hp: Spongiotic dermatitis, often with eosinophils - indistinguishable from other eczemas; the distribution and patch test make the diagnosis.
dx.assoc: Delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity in a distribution matching the allergen (nickel, fragrance, preservatives, rubber); patch testing identifies the culprit.
dx.mgmt: Identify and avoid the allergen; topical corticosteroids for localized disease and a tapering oral course for severe or widespread reactions.

dx.look: Stinging and smarting before itch. Erythema progressing to vesicles, erosions, crusting and scaling, strictly confined to the area of exposure and never spreading. Hands most often, occupational, cumulative. Occurs in anyone above a threshold dose.
fr: Stinging or burning before itching
Rapid onset, within hours of exposure
Sharply confined to the exposed area, never spreads
No papules in the acute phase
Wet work, detergents, solvents, cement; hands
ag: Delayed onset over days
Spread beyond the contact area
Occurs at trivially low exposure
dx.cf: History and site. Patch testing is still worth doing, because allergic contact dermatitis is frequently superimposed on chronic irritant hand dermatitis — the cement worker sensitized to chromate is the classic example.
dx.hp: Spongiosis with upper-epidermal necrosis and neutrophils in acute strong-irritant reactions; often indistinguishable from allergic contact dermatitis.
dx.assoc: Dose-dependent barrier damage (wet work, soaps, solvents), most often on the hands; no prior sensitization is needed, and patch tests to relevant allergens are negative.
dx.mgmt: Restore the barrier - reduce exposure, gloves, emollients - with a topical corticosteroid during flares.

dx.look: Ill-defined erythema with greasy yellow scale in sebaceous areas: scalp, eyebrows, glabella, nasolabial folds, retroauricular, presternal, and body folds. Mild itch. In body folds, a sharply marginated bright red exudative eruption with fissuring.
fr: Sebaceous distribution: scalp, brows, nasolabial folds, presternal
Greasy yellow-orange scale
Waxes and wanes, worse in winter and with stress
Mild itch relative to appearance
ag: Flexural antecubital and popliteal distribution
Severe itch dominating
Geometric outlines
dx.cf: Clinical. Test for HIV if severe, extensive or refractory. In infants consider Langerhans cell histiocytosis if there is purpura, and zinc deficiency if there is a perioral and perianal accentuation.
dx.hp: Spongiosis with parakeratosis at the follicular ostia and a superficial perivascular infiltrate.
dx.assoc: Malassezia-driven; severe or refractory disease is an HIV marker and is more common in Parkinson disease.
dx.mgmt: Topical ketoconazole with a low-potency corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor; antifungal shampoos for the scalp.

dx.look: Ferocious itch, characteristically worse at night, with burrows in finger webs, flexor wrists, axillary folds, periumbilical skin, areolae and genitals. Papules, excoriations and secondary eczematization. Household contacts itch too. In infants, palms, soles and scalp are involved.
fr: Itch markedly worse at night
Household or institutional contacts also itching
Burrows in finger webs and flexor wrists
Genital or areolar nodules
Spares the head in adults
ag: No contacts affected
Itch unrelated to time of day
Strictly localized to one contact area
dx.cf: Skin scraping in mineral oil from a burrow or papule, examined for mites, eggs or feces. Dermoscopy shows the delta-wing jet sign at the burrow's end and is quicker and more acceptable to the patient than scraping.
dx.dsc: The delta-wing jet sign - a small dark triangle (the mite head) at the end of a burrow - is diagnostic on dermoscopy.
dx.hp: Mite parts, eggs or feces in the stratum corneum with a spongiotic, eosinophil-rich dermal reaction when a burrow is sampled.
dx.assoc: Intensely itchy, worse at night, with burrows in web spaces, wrists and genitals; treat all close contacts simultaneously. Crusted (Norwegian) scabies signals immunosuppression.
dx.mgmt: Topical permethrin 5% (repeat in one week) or oral ivermectin; treat all household and sexual contacts and decontaminate bedding and clothing.

dx.look: Older adult, medial lower leg above the malleolus, with erythema, scaling, weeping, hemosiderin brown pigmentation, varicosities and pitting edema. Often bilateral though asymmetric. Progresses to lipodermatosclerosis and ulceration.
fr: Medial lower leg above the ankle
Hemosiderin brown pigmentation
Pitting edema and varicose veins
Bilateral, though often asymmetric
Improves with elevation and compression
ag: Unilateral with fever and rapid spread — that is cellulitis
Involvement of arms or trunk
dx.cf: Clinical, with Doppler ankle-brachial pressure index before compression. Patch test when it fails to improve — allergic contact dermatitis to topical antibiotics, lanolin and rubber in bandages is extremely common in this population.
dx.hp: A lobular capillary proliferation in the papillary dermis with hemosiderin, extravasated red cells and dermal fibrosis - clues to chronic venous change.
dx.assoc: Chronic venous insufficiency (ankle edema, varicosities, medial-ankle hemosiderin); frequently misread as cellulitis when it is bilateral. Assess for venous disease and heart failure.
dx.mgmt: Compression and leg elevation are the cornerstone, with emollients and a topical corticosteroid for the eczema; treat the underlying venous insufficiency.

dx.look: Coin-shaped plaques of coalesced vesicles and papules, weeping or crusted, intensely pruritic, on the extensor legs and dorsal hands of older adults with dry skin, in winter.
fr: Discrete coin-shaped plaques
Marked xerosis of surrounding skin
Winter onset, older adult
Intense itch
ag: Central clearing with an active edge
Flexural pattern with atopic history
dx.cf: KOH to exclude tinea, which it mimics closely. Patch test if it persists — nummular lesions can be an expression of contact allergy.
dx.dsc: Patchy dotted vessels with yellowish serocrust in a nonspecific eczematous pattern; used mainly to help exclude tinea.
dx.hp: Spongiotic dermatitis with acanthosis and a serum-scale crust; biopsy serves to exclude tinea or mycosis fungoides.
dx.assoc: Background xerosis and atopy; nickel or other contact allergy can drive persistent lesions - patch test refractory cases, and exclude tinea with KOH.
dx.mgmt: Liberal emollients with a mid- to high-potency topical corticosteroid; treat secondary staphylococcal infection and correct the dry skin.

dx.look: Crops of deep-seated, intensely itchy, tapioca-like vesicles on the lateral fingers, palms and soles, without much surrounding erythema. Recurrent, often seasonal, resolving with desquamation and collarettes.
fr: Deep-seated tapioca vesicles on lateral fingers and palms
Little surrounding erythema
Recurrent in crops, often seasonal
Intense itch preceding the vesicles
ag: Unilateral — always exclude tinea manuum in one-hand disease
Scaling annular border
dx.cf: KOH from the vesicle roof to exclude tinea manuum, which classically produces one-hand two-feet disease. Patch test for nickel and cobalt if recurrent.
dx.hp: Spongiotic vesicles within the thick acral epidermis without acantholysis; KOH excludes a vesicular id reaction to tinea.
dx.assoc: Deep-seated tapioca vesicles on the lateral fingers, palms and soles; triggers include stress, sweating, nickel and an id reaction to distant tinea.
dx.mgmt: High-potency topical corticosteroids and emollients with cool soaks in acute flares; address triggers, and use phototherapy or systemic agents for refractory disease.

dx.look: A well-defined plaque of thickened skin with exaggerated skin markings (lichenification) and variable hyperpigmentation, at a site the patient can reach and habitually rubs: nape, ankle, wrist, scrotum, vulva, anogenital.
fr: Solitary or few plaques at reachable sites
Exaggerated skin lines within a leathery plaque
Patient acknowledges rubbing, often unconsciously and at night
Long-standing and stable
ag: Widespread symmetric involvement
Vesicles or weeping
dx.cf: Clinical. Look for the underlying itch it grew from — atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, tinea, neuropathic itch. Treating the plaque without breaking the itch-scratch cycle will not work.
dx.hp: Compact hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, irregular acanthosis with elongated rete, and vertical papillary-dermal fibrosis from chronic rubbing.
dx.assoc: A secondary lichenification from the itch-scratch cycle - look for an underlying dermatosis (atopic eczema, tinea, neuropathy) and contributing stress.
dx.mgmt: Break the itch-scratch cycle - a potent topical corticosteroid (occluded or intralesional) with barrier and behavioral measures; treat any underlying cause.

dx.look: An adult with a persistent, asymmetric, oddly shaped scaly dermatitis in sun-protected sites, present for years, that has never fully cleared on adequate topical steroid and has been labeled eczema throughout.
fr: Adult onset with no atopic history
Persistent for years despite treatment
Asymmetric, bizarre outlines
Bathing-trunk or sun-protected distribution
Poikiloderma
ag: Complete clearance on topical steroid
Childhood onset with atopic history
dx.cf: Repeated biopsies from untreated sites with T cell receptor gene rearrangement. Stop topical steroids for 2–4 weeks first.
dx.dsc: Fine short linear vessels with orange-yellow patches; asymmetric and persistent.
dx.hp: Epidermotropic atypical lymphocytes with Pautrier microabscesses; repeat biopsies off topical steroids are often needed.
dx.assoc: Persistent eczema or psoriasis that never fully clears in a sun-protected distribution; send T-cell receptor gene rearrangement and refer.
dx.mgmt: Skin-directed therapy (topical steroids, nitrogen mustard, bexarotene, phototherapy) for early stage; specialist cutaneous-lymphoma referral.

dx.look: A dermatophyte infection that has been treated as eczema or psoriasis, so the ring has been flattened and blurred. Scale is scanty, the color is deep red or violaceous, the outline is irregular and asymmetric, and follicular papules and pustules stud the plaque. Steroid atrophy and telangiectasia sit on top. It settles for a few days with each application and then extends further.
fr: Improves briefly on a topical steroid, then spreads further
Irregular asymmetric outline with a raised edge somewhere in the plaque
Follicular papules or pustules within the plaque
Minimal scale with steroid-induced atrophy and telangiectasia
Coexisting tinea pedis, onychomycosis or groin involvement
One hand, one foot, or a single fold affected
ag: Symmetric flexural disease since childhood
Complete and sustained clearance on a topical steroid
Negative KOH from an untreated advancing edge
dx.cf: KOH and fungal culture from the advancing edge, ideally after 2 weeks off topical steroid and antifungal. If treatment cannot wait, a biopsy with PAS staining is more sensitive than KOH in steroid-modified disease. Always look at the feet and toenails of anyone with an odd asymmetric plaque.
dx.dsc: Broken, bent and comma-shaped hairs within the plaque, with a peripheral scaling edge and follicular pustules - a useful pointer when scale has been suppressed.
dx.hp: Hyphae in the stratum corneum on PAS or methenamine silver staining, with neutrophils in a compact or parakeratotic horn; folliculocentric involvement indicates dermatophytic folliculitis or Majocchi granuloma.
dx.assoc: Caused by topical corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor applied to an undiagnosed dermatophytosis, often bought over the counter or borrowed from a relative. Extension down the follicle produces Majocchi granuloma, which will not clear on topical therapy.
dx.mgmt: Stop the steroid. Topical terbinafine or an azole for purely epidermal disease; oral terbinafine or itraconazole when follicles, nails, palms, soles or a large area are involved. Treat the feet and nails at the same time and check household contacts, or it returns immediately.

dx.look: Firm, dome-shaped 5 to 20 mm nodules with eroded, crusted or warty tops, scattered symmetrically on the extensor limbs, shoulders and upper back, with normal-looking skin between them. Lesions occur only where the hands can reach, so the mid-upper back is spared in a butterfly-shaped island. The itch is described as piercing or burning, and it wakes people at night.
fr: Discrete firm nodules with excoriated or crusted tops
Extensor limbs and shoulders, symmetric, with normal skin between
Sparing of the unreachable mid-upper back
Piercing itch that drives picking and disturbs sleep
Lesions persist for months after the scratching stops
Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and scarring at healed sites
ag: Confluent plaques rather than discrete nodules
A single plaque at one reachable site
Itch that settles completely with a short steroid course
dx.cf: Clinical. The real work is finding the driver: about half are atopic, and the rest need a systemic itch screen - CBC, ferritin, renal and liver function, thyroid, HbA1c, HIV and a chest radiograph. Biopsy an atypical nodule to exclude keratoacanthoma, hypertrophic lichen planus and pemphigoid nodularis.
dx.hp: Marked irregular pseudoepitheliomatous epidermal hyperplasia with compact hyperkeratosis, vertically streaked thickened papillary dermal collagen, and increased dermal nerve fibers.
dx.assoc: Atopic dermatitis in around half. Otherwise chronic kidney disease, cholestasis, iron deficiency, thyroid disease, HIV, lymphoma, and neuropathic or psychiatric drivers. Itch that persists after adequate topical treatment usually means the underlying cause has not been found.
dx.mgmt: Intralesional triamcinolone or a superpotent topical corticosteroid under occlusion, with a sedating antihistamine at night to break the scratch cycle. Escalate to phototherapy, gabapentin, dupilumab or a JAK inhibitor. Treat the underlying cause and address the anxiety that sustains the habit.

dx.n: Photoallergic and phototoxic dermatitis (including chronic actinic dermatitis)
dx.look: Eczematous dermatitis confined to light-exposed skin - face, V of the neck, dorsal hands and forearms - with a knife-sharp cut-off at the collar and sleeve. The giveaway is sparing of the shaded areas: upper eyelids, the strip under the nose, the groove below the lower lip, and behind the ears. Phototoxic reactions look like an exaggerated sunburn with vesicles; photoallergic reactions look like allergic contact dermatitis and can spread onto covered skin.
fr: Sharp cut-off at collar, sleeve and sock lines
Sparing of upper eyelids, submental skin and the area under the nose
Retroauricular sparing
Started after a new systemic drug, sunscreen, fragrance or antibacterial
Worse in summer and within a day or two of sun exposure
Severe lichenified plaques on the face and hands of an older man
ag: Involvement of covered skin only
Sharp geometric borders unrelated to sun exposure
No seasonal or sunlight relationship at all
dx.cf: Photopatch testing: a duplicate allergen series, one set irradiated with UVA at 24 hours, both read at 48 and 96 hours. A reaction only at the irradiated site confirms photoallergy. Add monochromatic phototesting for suspected chronic actinic dermatitis, and check ANA and ENA to exclude lupus.
dx.hp: Epidermal spongiosis with a lymphocytic infiltrate in photoallergy. Phototoxic lesions show sunburn cells and upper epidermal necrosis rather than spongiosis. Chronic actinic dermatitis shows a dense, sometimes pseudolymphomatous dermal infiltrate that can mimic mycosis fungoides.
dx.assoc: Common culprits are thiazides, doxycycline, amiodarone, piroxicam and naproxen, quinolones, chlorpromazine, and topical sunscreens, fragrances and antibacterials. Photoallergy can evolve into chronic actinic dermatitis, which then persists independently of the original agent. Consider HIV testing in a younger adult with chronic actinic dermatitis.
dx.mgmt: Identify and stop the agent, then rigorous photoprotection - broad-spectrum high-SPF sunscreen, clothing, window film. Stopping the drug alone will not clear chronic actinic dermatitis. Topical corticosteroids for the dermatitis, escalating to azathioprine, cyclosporine or mycophenolate for severe persistent disease.

dx.look: Crops of discrete red-brown scaly or crusted papules and small papulovesicles scattered over the central chest, back and flanks, sparing the face and distal limbs. They feel like sandpaper under the fingers and itch out of all proportion to how little there is to see. Typically a man over 40 after sweating, sun exposure, a febrile illness or a period of bed rest.
fr: Discrete keratotic papules with a sandpaper feel on the central trunk
Man over 40 with itch out of proportion to the visible eruption
Provoked by heat, sweating, sun, fever or bed rest
Spares the face and distal limbs
Waxes and wanes in crops over weeks to months
ag: Flexural distribution with a childhood atopic history
Greasy scale confined to sebaceous areas
Burrows, or household contacts who also itch
dx.cf: Biopsy an intact papule - the diagnosis is histologic, and the clinical picture is routinely mislabeled folliculitis, miliaria or 'nonspecific eczema'. Focal acantholysis with dyskeratosis in one of four patterns settles it, and negative direct immunofluorescence excludes pemphigus.
dx.hp: Focal suprabasal or subcorneal acantholysis with dyskeratosis (corps ronds and grains) confined to small foci on a background of spongiosis; direct immunofluorescence is negative.
dx.assoc: Heat, sweating, ultraviolet exposure, prolonged bed rest and febrile illness are the triggers. Reported with hematologic and solid malignancies and with some chemotherapies, but a cancer hunt is not indicated in an otherwise well person. Persistent forms exist despite the name.
dx.mgmt: Keep cool and avoid sweating, then a mid- to high-potency topical corticosteroid with emollients. Add a topical vitamin D analog, phototherapy or an oral retinoid for persistent disease. Oral corticosteroids give short-lived relief and it relapses on withdrawal.
dx.pat: Central trunk, spares face and limbs

dx.look: Sudden painful deterioration of established eczema, with crops of monomorphic 2 to 3 mm punched-out erosions and hemorrhagic crusts studded through the eczematous skin, most often on face, neck and upper trunk. Unlike ordinary herpes the lesions are disseminated within the dermatosis rather than grouped, and successive crops appear over days with fever and lymphadenopathy.
fr: Monomorphic, uniformly sized punched-out erosions
Painful rather than itchy - the symptom quality has changed
Sudden deterioration of previously stable eczema
Fever, malaise and tender lymphadenopathy
Contact with a household member who has cold sores
Failure to improve on antibiotics alone
ag: Polymorphic lesions of differing sizes and ages
Honey-colored crust without discrete punched-out erosions
No pain and no systemic upset
dx.cf: Viral PCR or direct fluorescent antibody from the base of a freshly deroofed lesion is fast and definitive, and a Tzanck smear gives an answer in minutes. Do not wait for any of them - start acyclovir on suspicion. Send a bacterial swab alongside, because staphylococcal co-infection is usual.
dx.hp: Ballooning degeneration with multinucleate keratinocytes and steel-gray nuclear inclusions, on a background of spongiotic dermatitis.
dx.assoc: Atopic dermatitis is the usual host, but also Darier disease, Hailey-Hailey disease, pemphigus, burns, ichthyosis and cutaneous T cell lymphoma. Complications are keratoconjunctivitis with corneal ulceration, staphylococcal bacteremia, and disseminated infection in infants and the immunosuppressed.
dx.mgmt: Systemic acyclovir - intravenous if extensive, febrile, periocular, or in an infant. Add antistaphylococcal cover for the near-universal secondary infection and obtain an urgent ophthalmology opinion for any periocular involvement. Continue emollients, and restart topical corticosteroids once the virus is controlled.

dx.n: Acquired zinc deficiency and acrodermatitis enteropathica
dx.look: Sharply marginated, brightly red, dry scaly plaques that become vesiculobullous, eroded and crusted, first around the mouth, anus and genitals, then on hands, feet, scalp and flexures. Fingertips look glistening and fissured with paronychia, there is angular cheilitis and a red glossy tongue, and it is completed by diffuse alopecia, diarrhea and a miserable, whining, irritable child.
fr: Periorificial and acral distribution - perioral, anogenital, hands and feet
Sharply marginated bright red eroded and crusted plaques
Glistening fissured fingertips with paronychia and angular cheilitis
Diffuse alopecia and diarrhea
Alcohol dependence, malabsorption, bariatric surgery or parenteral nutrition
In infants, onset after weaning or on bovine milk formula
ag: A normal zinc level on a properly collected sample in mild disease
Flexural distribution with a lifelong atopic history
No mucosal, hair or gastrointestinal involvement
dx.cf: Serum or plasma zinc in a trace-element tube, with alkaline phosphatase as a zinc-dependent surrogate. Hypoalbuminemia and acute inflammation both lower the measured level, so a borderline result in a convincing picture should not stop treatment. The response to replacement is the real test.
dx.hp: Confluent parakeratosis with pallor and ballooning of the upper epidermis and necrosis of the upper third - the same nutritional deficiency pattern seen in pellagra and necrolytic migratory erythema.
dx.assoc: Inherited (SLC39A4 mutation, presenting after weaning) or acquired through alcohol dependence, malabsorption, inflammatory bowel disease, bariatric surgery, anorexia or unsupplemented parenteral nutrition. When the same pattern occurs with a normal zinc level, think glucagonoma syndrome, pellagra and biotin deficiency.
dx.mgmt: Elemental zinc at two to three times the daily requirement, orally or intravenously. Diarrhea and irritability improve within 24 hours and the skin heals within 1 to 2 weeks, which treats and confirms at the same time. Correct the underlying cause and monitor copper on long-term supplementation.

ctx.l: Onset in infancy or early childhood
Hands are the main or only site
ctx.s: Most chronic irritant contact dermatitis is on the hands and occupational, Fitzpatrick 8e §2

ctx.l: Wet work, detergents, solvents or cement exposure
Personal or family history of asthma or hay fever
Venous insufficiency, varicose veins or leg edema
Applying topical antibiotic, lanolin or a bandage to the area
ctx.s: Neomycin and bacitracin are among the top contact allergens, Fitzpatrick 8e §2 Table 2-2

ctx.l: Present for more than 3 years without ever clearing
ctx.s: Chronicity without clearance is the key alert for MF

ctx.l: Known eczema and a household member with cold sores
ctx.s: Eczema herpeticum is often transmitted from parental herpes labialis, Fitzpatrick 8e §27

ctx.l: Alcohol dependence, bariatric surgery, malabsorption or parenteral nutrition

find.l: Flexural antecubital and popliteal distribution
Sharply marginated to an area of contact, geometric or linear
Spread beyond the original contact area
find.s: Spreading distinguishes allergic from irritant contact dermatitis, Fitzpatrick 8e §2 Table 2-3

find.l: Stinging or burning came before the itch
Onset 12–72 hours after exposure, not within hours
Papules present in the acute phase
find.s: In acute contact dermatitis, papules occur only in the allergic form, Fitzpatrick 8e §2

find.l: Itch markedly worse at night
Burrows in finger webs, wrists, axillae or genitals
Greasy yellow scale in nasolabial folds and eyebrows
Hemosiderin brown pigmentation on the medial lower leg
Pitting edema with varicosities
Deep-seated tapioca-like vesicles on lateral fingers or palms
Coin-shaped discrete plaques on a background of xerosis
Leathery plaque with exaggerated skin lines at a reachable site
Asymmetric with bizarre, irregular outlines
Never clears completely on an adequate topical steroid
find.s: Failure to clear should always prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis

find.l: Xerosis and lichenification with Dennie-Morgan folds
Crazy-paving (crazed-porcelain) fissured pattern on xerotic shins
Symmetric distant eczema flaring with an active primary focus (e.g., tinea pedis)
Raised, advancing, scaly edge somewhere in the plaque despite steroid treatment
Follicular papules or pustules inside the plaque, on atrophic steroid-treated skin
find.s: Dermatophytic folliculitis and Majocchi granuloma, Fitzpatrick 8e §26

find.l: One hand or one foot involved with the other side entirely normal
find.s: One-hand two-feet disease is tinea until disproved, Fitzpatrick 8e §26

find.l: Discrete firm dome-shaped nodules with excoriated tops on extensor limbs
Mid-upper back spared in a butterfly-shaped island the hands cannot reach
Sharp cut-off at the collar and sleeve, sparing upper eyelids and the skin under the nose
Began after a new systemic drug, sunscreen, fragrance or antibacterial, and worse in summer
Crops of itchy keratotic papules with a sandpaper feel on the central trunk of an adult
Flares with heat, sweating, fever or a period of bed rest
Monomorphic 2 to 3 mm punched-out erosions studding eczematous skin
Abrupt painful deterioration of known eczema with fever and malaise
Sharply marginated red plaques around mouth, anus and genitals with glistening fissured fingertips
Angular cheilitis, diffuse alopecia and diarrhea accompanying the dermatitis
Distant eruption cleared once the primary focus was treated, with a negative scraping at the distant sites
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - the id reaction resolves when the primary focus is treated and is organism-negative

find.l: Flares every winter with dry indoor heating or hot soapy bathing, and settles on emollients alone
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - low humidity and overwashing precipitate asteatotic eczema

test.l: Patch testing (Finn chambers, read at 48 and 96 h)
test.w: Any dermatitis that is not improving as expected, all chronic hand and foot dermatitis, all stasis dermatitis failing treatment, any adult with new or changed atopic dermatitis, and eyelid, perianal and periorbital dermatitis.
test.p: A papulovesicular reaction confined to the test site at 96 hours identifies the allergen. Relevance must then be established against the patient's actual exposures — a positive patch test is not automatically the cause.
test.n: A negative series does not exclude contact allergy to something outside the standard series. Consider testing the patient's own products.
test.x: Delay until the dermatitis has been quiet for at least 2 weeks and apply to previously uninvolved skin. Testing on active or recently steroid-treated skin produces both false positives from angry back and false negatives from local suppression.

test.l: Skin scraping in mineral oil, or dermoscopy for burrows
test.w: Any itch that is worse at night, any itch with affected contacts, and any dermatitis of the finger webs, genitals or areolae.
test.p: Finding a mite, egg or fecal pellet is definitive. Treat the patient and every household and sexual contact simultaneously, whether or not they itch.
test.n: Sensitivity is low, because an ordinary infestation carries only 10–15 mites. A negative scraping in a convincing clinical picture does not exclude scabies — treat anyway.
test.x: Dermoscopy is faster, better tolerated, and better at locating the burrow: look for the dark triangular delta-wing jet sign at the leading end. Scrape where dermoscopy points.

test.w: Any annular, coin-shaped or one-handed dermatitis, and before any topical steroid on an undiagnosed scaly plaque.
test.p: Hyphae confirm dermatophytosis, which changes the treatment entirely.
test.n: Reduces but does not eliminate tinea, particularly after topical steroid use.
test.x: One-hand, two-feet involvement is tinea manuum until disproved, however much it resembles dyshidrotic eczema.

test.l: Skin biopsy with T cell receptor gene rearrangement
test.w: Adult-onset dermatitis persisting for years without complete clearance, asymmetric or bizarre outlines, or a sun-protected distribution.
test.p: Epidermotropism with Pautrier microabscesses and a clonal T cell population supports mycosis fungoides. Stage and refer.
test.n: A single negative biopsy does not exclude early MF. Repeat over time from different sites — that is standard practice, not diagnostic failure.
test.x: Stop topical steroids for 2–4 weeks first, or the infiltrate will be suppressed and the biopsy wasted.

test.l: Bacterial swab for culture and sensitivity
test.w: Weeping, crusted or pustular eczema, sudden deterioration, or failure to respond to adequate topical therapy.
test.p: Identifies Staphylococcus aureus and its sensitivities. In dermatitis that suddenly worsens, superinfection is the commonest reason.
test.n: Colonization is near-universal in atopic dermatitis, so a positive culture is not automatically the explanation. Weigh it against the clinical picture.
test.x: If the erosions are monomorphic and punched-out, this is eczema herpeticum, not impetiginization. Send a viral PCR alongside and start acyclovir — antibiotics alone will not touch it.

test.s: Standard vascular assessment before compression therapy
test.w: Before applying compression to any leg. Compression on an ischemic limb causes tissue loss.
test.p: An index above 0.8 permits full compression. Between 0.5 and 0.8, use reduced compression with vascular input. Below 0.5, do not compress and refer urgently.
test.n: A normal index confirms compression is safe, which is the intervention that actually treats stasis dermatitis.
test.x: Falsely high readings occur in diabetes and chronic kidney disease from medial calcification. Use toe pressures or waveform analysis in those patients.

test.l: Viral PCR or direct fluorescent antibody from a deroofed erosion
test.w: Any eczema that suddenly worsens, becomes painful, develops uniform punched-out erosions, or fails to respond to antibiotics.
test.p: Detection of herpes simplex confirms eczema herpeticum. Continue acyclovir, check the eyes, and treat the coexisting staphylococcal infection.
test.n: A negative result from an old crusted lesion is unreliable. Sample a fresh vesicle or the base of a recent erosion, and do not stop acyclovir on the strength of a single negative in a convincing picture.
test.x: The recurring error is swabbing for bacteria only, finding Staphylococcus aureus, and treating with antibiotics alone while the virus disseminates. Send both, and start acyclovir before either result comes back.

test.l: KOH and fungal culture from the advancing edge, off topical steroid
test.w: Any asymmetric, one-sided or oddly shaped dermatitis, any plaque that flares whenever the steroid is stopped, and every undiagnosed scaly plaque before a steroid is prescribed.
test.p: Hyphae or a positive culture confirms dermatophytosis and changes the treatment completely. Follicular involvement or nail disease means oral rather than topical therapy.
test.n: A negative KOH after recent steroid or antifungal use does not exclude it. Stop both for 2 weeks and repeat, or biopsy with a PAS stain, which is more sensitive in steroid-modified disease.
test.x: Sampling the flat center rather than the raised edge is the standard reason for a false negative. Scrape the advancing margin, and always inspect the feet and toenails for the reservoir.

test.l: Photopatch testing with a duplicate irradiated series
test.w: Eczematous dermatitis with a photodistribution, particularly when it began after a new drug or topical product, or when ordinary patch testing has been negative.
test.p: An eczematous reaction at the irradiated site but not the covered duplicate confirms photoallergy to that agent. Stopping it, plus photoprotection, is the treatment.
test.n: A negative result does not exclude photosensitivity - phototoxic reactions, drug photosensitivity and chronic actinic dermatitis all photopatch negative. Move on to monochromatic phototesting.
test.x: Running only a standard patch series in a photodistributed dermatitis is the common miss, because the allergen is inert until irradiated. The other trap is testing on a tanned or actively inflamed back.

test.l: Skin biopsy of an intact papule for focal acantholysis
test.w: Itchy discrete keratotic papules on the trunk of an adult, especially a man over 40, that have been labeled folliculitis or nonspecific eczema and have not responded.
test.p: Focal acantholysis with dyskeratosis confirms Grover disease. That ends the search, permits an honest explanation of the trigger factors, and directs treatment at heat avoidance rather than allergen hunting.
test.n: A negative biopsy from an excoriated or treated lesion is common because the changes are focal. Sample an intact papule, and repeat if the clinical picture is convincing.
test.x: Send a specimen for direct immunofluorescence at the same time. Acantholysis without a biopsy for immunofluorescence leaves pemphigus foliaceus and Hailey-Hailey disease unexcluded.

test.l: Serum zinc with alkaline phosphatase, and a therapeutic replacement trial
test.w: Periorificial and acral eczematous or erosive dermatitis, especially with diarrhea, alopecia, angular cheilitis or glossitis, and in any infant after weaning.
test.p: A low zinc with a low alkaline phosphatase confirms it. Replace immediately - the diarrhea and irritability settle within 24 hours and the skin within 1 to 2 weeks, which is itself confirmatory.
test.n: A normal level does not exclude tissue deficiency, since hypoalbuminemia, acute inflammation and hemodilution all distort it. If the picture fits, treat and watch the response.
test.x: Collection is the pitfall: use a trace-element tube, avoid rubber stoppers and hemolysis, and take the sample fasting. If zinc is normal and the eruption persists, look for glucagonoma syndrome, pellagra and biotin deficiency, which look identical.

test.l: Systemic screen for a cause of chronic itch
test.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin; accuracy figures are a calibrated estimate
test.w: Prurigo nodules in anyone without a clear atopic history, and in every case that fails to settle on adequate topical therapy.
test.p: CBC, ferritin, renal and liver function, thyroid function, HbA1c, HIV serology and a chest radiograph identify the treatable drivers - iron deficiency, cholestasis, uremia, thyroid disease, HIV and lymphoma. Correcting the driver is what stops the itch.
test.n: A normal screen supports a primary or atopic prurigo and justifies committing to phototherapy or a systemic agent rather than repeating investigations.
test.x: Treating the nodules while ignoring the itch guarantees recurrence. The nodule is the scar of the scratching, not the disease - if the itch is not addressed, new nodules simply appear beside the treated ones.

flag: When a dermatitis fails to improve on adequate treatment, the three explanations in order of frequency are: contact allergy to something being applied to it, unrecognized dermatophyte infection, and the diagnosis being wrong. Patch test, scrape, and biopsy — in that order.
